title: Hot Work — Cutting, Grinding, Welding and Soldering on Site
verdict:
No. I would not sign this and send a crew out on it, and the reason is one omission, not the citation work.

WHAT IS GOOD — and I checked it rather than assumed it. The JSON shape is exactly right: all twelve keys, no extras, no 'suggestFor', id 'hot-work' intact. Controls are highest-first in every one of the eleven steps. No residual exceeds its initial. No admin/PPE-only step claims low. The harness in a boom EWP is correctly labelled ppe, not engineering — the trap in the brief, and the author did not fall into it. On the law I pulled the current consolidations from legislation.qld.gov.au and read them: s 291 paragraphs (a), (d), (j), (k), (l), (o) are quoted VERBATIM and correctly; ss 299 (SWMS prepared), 300 (compliance), 301 (copy to principal contractor), 302 (review), 303 (kept) are each described correctly against their actual headings; s 51(2)(c) really does read 'the concentration of flammable gas, vapour, mist, or fumes exceeds 5% of the LEL'; s 53, ss 56/57 (LAeq,8h 85 dB(A), LC,peak 140 dB(C)), s 78, ss 44–46, ss 316/317 all check out. s 425(6) is right, and right in a way most people get wrong — Queensland's cut-off really is 'constructed after 31 December 1989', not 2003, and the SWMS carries that correctly while still telling you a pre-2004 building needs identification. s 427(2) is right. Every silica section exists as cited — 529B(1)(b) lists exactly the five control measures the SWMS names, 529BA, 529C, 529CA, 529CB, 529CC, 529CD, 529CE with its 14 days. Fire Services Act 1990 is in force under that name with Queensland Fire Department as the agency. Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 is in force (SL 2008 No. 160) and does carry the occupier's duties, and QDC MP 6.1 is real — s 50 and s 54(2) of that regulation mandate compliance with it by name. ANZCOR Guideline 9.1.5 exists under that exact title and says exactly what the emergency section says it says: 'This review has found no evidence to support this practice and it may be harmful.' The Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 is cited correctly and the dead 2013 instrument appears nowhere. This is a well-built document.

WHY IT STILL FAILS. Gaseous and special-hazard suppression is not mentioned once. Not FM-200, not Novec, not inert gas, not CO2 total flooding, not a release solenoid, not an actuator, not the word 'asphyxiation'. The activity line puts 'suppression isolated' in scope and the permits list names data centres, cold stores and hospitals — the exact rooms these systems protect. A crew grinding in a comms room trips the detection with their own smoke, the system discharges on them, and a CO2 or inert-gas discharge in that room is a killing mechanism, not an inconvenience. There is no step to put the release to manual-only or lock off the master cylinder actuator before the first spark, and — the mirror failure — no step in restoration to reconnect it and prove the release circuit, so the crew can also drive away leaving the room's real protection disconnected while the FIP reads normal. That is a fatal omission and it is squarely inside this company's trade.

Three more the author did not name: the fire pump. Step 3 leaves the controllers in AUTO, then step 6 has you open the drain — that pressure drop starts the jockey and then the main pump. Unexpected start, the rotating coupling, a diesel running in a sealed plant room (exhaust CO, and it will drown out the fire watch). Nowhere. Oxygen depletion: enrichment is covered well, depletion is absent — argon and CO2 shielding gas pooling in an unventilated plant room, and the gas detector control is LEL-only with no oxygen channel. EWP crush: the doc names 'striking sprinkler pipe and services overhead' as damage to the pipe, never as the operator crushed against it, and there is no ground person required to reach the emergency lowering controls and no rescue plan.

Two citations say something other than their source. s 52 is the wrong provision — s 52(2) reads 'This section does not apply if the ignition source is part of a deliberate process or activity at the workplace', which is precisely a welding arc, so s 52 does not reach the thing the control uses it for. The document even half-knows this: the hazard line in the same step says 'with a deliberate ignition source in your hand'. And the 24-hour critical defect rule is not AS 1851-2012, it is Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) s 53, with a 30 penalty unit maximum, a defined 'critical defect' in s 49, and two operative elements the SWMS drops — it goes to the OCCUPIER and it must be in the APPROVED FORM.

Two things I could not verify and neither should go out asserted as fact. The '8 hours maximum (AS 1674.1)' appears three times as a hard rule from a standard whose edition the document never states and which is paywalled — the references entry itself says to check the office copy before quoting it, then the body quotes a number from it anyway. And the QFD monitoring contractor is named as a specific company with a specific phone number plus a 12-hour approval threshold, in four places; qfd.qld.gov.au and worksafe.qld.gov.au are both unreachable from here, so none of it could be confirmed, and a named commercial contractor in a signed controlled document goes stale when the contract changes hands. I am not saying either is wrong. I am saying nobody has checked, and the document presents both as settled.

Also unverified, and not raised as findings because I have no reason to doubt them: the fourteen Queensland Code of Practice titles and years (worksafe.qld.gov.au is behind Cloudflare), and the AS numbers, which are paywalled. Someone with the office copies should tick those off before issue.

One usability note, not a finding: on a public-area EWP job with traffic this document simultaneously requires a dedicated fire watch with no other job, a spotter on the door and a spotter on the ground, and never states the minimum crew size. Say the number somewhere so a two-man crew knows before they leave the yard that this job is not a two-man job.

Fix the suppression-system omission and the two mis-citations, add the pump start, oxygen depletion and EWP crush, and downgrade the two unverified assertions to house rules pending a check, and I would sign this without hesitation. It is close.

blocking.field: steps[2] 'Isolate the fire system, book the monitoring off, and log it' — hazards and controls; also steps[9] 'Put the fire system back on and prove it works', permits, siteSpecificPrompts
blocking.problem: Gaseous and special-hazard suppression systems are absent from the entire document. Zero occurrences of gaseous, total flooding, FM-200, Novec, inert gas, CO2 system, special hazard, solenoid, actuator or asphyxiation. The activity line puts 'fire detection and suppression isolated' in scope and permits[3] names data centres, cold stores, hospitals and shopping centres — the rooms these systems protect. Hot work smoke and heat trips the detection, the system discharges onto the crew, and a CO2 or inert-gas total-flooding discharge is a lethal-atmosphere event, plus discharge overpressure and door blow-out. The isolation step has no control for putting the release to manual-only or locking off/removing the master cylinder actuator before the first spark, and the restoration step has no control for reconnecting the actuator and proving the release circuit — so the opposite failure, driving away with the room's suppression release disconnected while the FIP reads normal, is equally unaddressed.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[2] an 'isolate' level control: where the work area is protected by a gaseous, inert gas, CO2 or other special-hazard suppression system, place the release to manual-only and lock off or remove the actuator from the master cylinder, tag it with your own tag, record it on the impairment permit and the isolation register, and confirm the room's occupants and any adjoining rooms sharing the flood zone are informed. Add the discharge hazard to steps[2] hazards: accidental discharge of a total-flooding agent onto the work party — hypoxic atmosphere from CO2 and inert gas, overpressure and disorientation. Add a matching control at steps[9]: refit and reconnect the actuator, prove the release circuit and confirm the panel shows the release armed and in normal, photograph it, and include it in the second person's witnessed countersign. Add to permits: gaseous suppression isolation recorded on the impairment permit. Add to siteSpecificPrompts: 'Is the work area protected by a gaseous, inert gas or CO2 total-flooding system? Who locks off the actuator, and who proves it is back and armed before you leave?' Add a line to emergency covering unintended agent discharge: get out, do not re-enter until ventilated and the atmosphere is proved, ring 000 if anyone was in the room.

blocking.field: steps[5] 'Prepare the pipe — drain it, prove it, test the air, and know what is in it' — hazards; and steps[2] controls[0] which leaves the pump controllers in AUTO
blocking.problem: The automatic fire pump is never named as a hazard. steps[2] controls[0] says 'Leave the fire pump controllers in AUTO unless the work itself requires otherwise', and steps[5] controls[0] then has the technician open the drain and the test valve. On most sprinkler and hydrant installations that pressure drop starts the jockey pump and then the main pump. Nothing in the document names unexpected pump start, contact with the rotating shaft or coupling, a diesel pump running in an enclosed plant room (carbon monoxide from the exhaust, heat, and noise well above the exposure standard the document itself cites at ss 56 and 57 — which will also stop the fire watch hearing anything), or the need to confirm the pump cannot drive water into the section the technician is cut into.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[5] hazards: 'Fire pump starts automatically on the pressure drop when the section is drained — rotating shaft and coupling, diesel exhaust and noise in an enclosed plant room, and water driven back toward the open section.' Add an 'isolate' level control to steps[5] before the existing controls[0]: agree with the building's responsible person what happens to the pump controller for the duration, and either confirm the locked shut section valve positively prevents the pump feeding the open section, or take the controller out of AUTO under the electrical isolation permit already listed in permits, record it on the impairment permit and restore it in steps[9] with the witness present. Add an 'engineering' control: guards in place over the pump coupling, nobody within reach of the coupling while the controller is in AUTO, and the plant room ventilated or the roller door open before a diesel pump can run. Add to steps[9] controls: confirm the pump controller is back in AUTO, the pump is not in a run or fail state and the panel shows no pump fault. Add to siteSpecificPrompts: 'Will draining this section start the pump, and what is being done about it?'

blocking.field: steps[5] controls[2] and controls[3], steps[7] hazards, training entry on the flammable gas detector, ppe
blocking.problem: Oxygen depletion is nowhere in the document. Oxygen ENRICHMENT is covered well (steps[7] hazards, and the control forbidding oxygen for ventilating or blowing down), and CO2 extinguisher discharge in a small plant room is covered in emergency — but nothing covers oxygen being displaced. GMAW shielding gas is argon or an argon/CO2 mix, both heavier than air, and the document contemplates arc welding in 'a small unventilated room'. A leaking or knocked-open cylinder left in a plant room, or purge gas, will do the same. The gas test control is LEL-only: 'The reading must be below 5% of the LEL', with no oxygen channel and no oxygen acceptance criterion, so a technician using a single-gas LEL detector will read clear in an atmosphere that is already short of oxygen.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[7] hazards: 'Oxygen displaced by shielding gas, purge gas or a leaking cylinder in a small or unventilated plant room — argon and CO2 are heavier than air and pool at low level; a flammable-gas detector reads clear in an oxygen-deficient atmosphere.' Amend steps[5] controls[2] so the instrument is a multi-gas detector reading oxygen as well as LEL, with an acceptance criterion of oxygen between 19.5% and 23.5% alongside the below-5%-LEL criterion, both written on the permit. Amend steps[5] controls[3] so the stop trigger is either 5% LEL or oxygen outside 19.5–23.5%. Amend the training entry on the detector to cover reading the oxygen channel and what to do when it alarms. Amend steps[7] controls[2] so the forced ventilation requirement is stated as protecting against oxygen displacement as well as fume. Add to emergency: signs of oxygen deficiency and the rule that nobody enters to retrieve a collapsed workmate without the atmosphere being proved.

blocking.field: steps[5] 'Prepare the pipe — drain it, prove it, test the air, and know what is in it' — controls[2], the third control, second sentence
blocking.problem: The control states: 'An atmosphere at or above 5% LEL is a hazardous atmosphere under WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 51(2)(c), and s 52 makes an ignition source in it something you must control — in plain terms, you do not strike an arc in it.' s 52 says the opposite of what is claimed. Verified at legislation.qld.gov.au, current consolidation: 's 52 Ignition sources (1) A person conducting a business or undertaking at a workplace must manage risks to health and safety associated with an ignition source in a hazardous atmosphere at the workplace under part 3.1. ... (2) This section does not apply if the ignition source is part of a deliberate process or activity at the workplace.' A welding arc, an oxy flame and a grinder are deliberate processes, so s 52 expressly does not apply to them — the document has cited the one provision that carves out exactly the ignition source the step is about. The document contradicts itself here: the hazard line in the same step correctly says 'with a deliberate ignition source in your hand'. Separately, s 51(2)(c) reads 'exceeds 5% of the LEL', not 'at or above', so the paraphrase is also not what the section says (the step's own hazards entry gets this right with 'once it exceeds 5% of the LEL').
blocking.fix: Delete the reference to s 52 from this control. Replace the sentence with: 'An atmosphere in which the concentration of flammable gas, vapour, mist or fumes exceeds 5% of the LEL is a hazardous atmosphere under WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 51(2)(c), and s 51(1) requires that risk to be managed under part 3.1. In plain terms, you do not strike an arc in it.' Keep the operational stop trigger at 5% — being conservative on the number is right, it just is not what s 51(2)(c) says. Consider dropping the s 52 line from references as well, or leaving it there only as the bare provision title it already carries, since s 52 does not bear on deliberate hot work.

blocking.field: steps[10] 'Clean up, close the permit and report' — controls[4], the defect reporting control
blocking.problem: The control states: 'AS 1851-2012 requires the responsible entity to be told of a critical defect before you leave site and confirmed in writing within 24 hours.' In Queensland this is a statutory duty on the person doing the maintenance, not a standard, and the document points the technician at the wrong instrument. Verified at legislation.qld.gov.au: Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) s 53 'Notifying critical defects — (1) This section applies if a person who is carrying out, or has carried out, maintenance of a prescribed fire safety installation for a building, becomes aware, or ought reasonably to be aware, of a critical defect in the installation. (2) The person must give the occupier of the building a notice about the defect in the approved form (a critical defect notice) within 24 hours after the person carries out the maintenance of the installation. Maximum penalty—30 penalty units.' 'Critical defect' is defined at s 49. The SWMS drops both operative elements: the notice goes to the OCCUPIER, and it must be in the APPROVED FORM. A technician following this control as written emails the office and thinks they are done.
blocking.fix: Rewrite controls[4] as: 'Any defect you could not rectify goes on the job card and to the office the same day. If it is a critical defect — one likely to render the installation inoperable and reasonably likely to have a significant adverse impact on occupant safety in a fire (Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) s 49) — you must give the OCCUPIER a critical defect notice in the approved form within 24 hours of doing the maintenance (Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) s 53). Tell them face to face before you leave site as well. AS 1851-2012 also carries defect reporting and recording obligations — follow both.' Add to references: 'Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) s 49 — meaning of critical defect; s 53 — notifying critical defects (notice to the occupier in the approved form within 24 hours); s 50 and s 54(2) — maintenance in compliance with QDC part MP6.1.'

blocking.field: whenRequired (third paragraph), permits[0], steps[0] controls[2] — the '8 hours maximum (AS 1674.1)' claim; and references entry for AS 1674.1
blocking.problem: The document asserts three times, as a hard rule sourced to AS 1674.1, that a hot work permit runs to a maximum of 8 hours. It also sources the 15 m hot work area, the post-work inspection, the no-lone-welding rule and blowpipe lighting practice to the same standard. None of this could be verified in this review — AS 1674.1 is paywalled, store.standards.org.au returns no readable catalogue data, and the document never states which edition it is relying on. The document's own references entry concedes the point — 'Check the edition and clause numbers in the copy held in the office before quoting a clause number to anybody' — and then the body quotes a substantive number from that standard anyway. The 8-hour figure is the one that changes what a crew does on the day, and I could not confirm AS 1674.1 sets it rather than it being common insurer or site practice. The document handles this honestly for the 60-minute fire watch at steps[8] controls[3] ('AS 1674.1 requires the area to be inspected... it does not set the length of the watch for you... The Safe QLD rule is 60') and should handle the permit clock the same way.
blocking.fix: Before issue, have someone open the office copy of AS 1674.1, record the edition (state it everywhere the standard is cited, e.g. 'AS 1674.1-1997'), and confirm whether the standard sets a maximum permit currency and the 15 m hot work area. If it does, keep the attribution and add the edition. If it does not, rewrite whenRequired, permits[0] and steps[0] controls[2] to read as the Safe QLD and insurer rule — for example 'The Safe QLD rule is that a hot work permit runs to a maximum of 8 hours, and a new permit is required if the work stops for more than 2 hours or runs past the finish time on it' — with AS 1674.1 named for fire precautions generally and without a number attached to it. Do not delete the 8-hour rule; it is good practice either way. Only the attribution is at risk.

blocking.field: permits[2], steps[2] controls[2], references (QFD alarm monitoring entry), siteSpecificPrompts entries on the ASE reference and the 12-hour question
blocking.problem: The document names a specific commercial monitoring contractor and a specific phone number ('Johnson Controls, 1300 360 575') as THE QFD monitoring contractor, and states a 12-hour threshold above which a QFD approval is required, in four separate places, all as settled fact. None of it could be verified: qfd.qld.gov.au is rejected at the gateway and worksafe.qld.gov.au is behind a Cloudflare challenge from this environment, so the regulator's own alarm-monitoring publication was unreachable. I confirmed the surrounding law is real — Fire Services Act 1990 (Qld) s 146N places the unwanted-alarm duty on the occupier and expressly contemplates 'establishing requirements for persons working near the system to isolate the system while using tools that may cause an unwanted alarm' — but nothing in the Act sets a 12-hour figure, so that threshold and the contractor's identity are both policy, and policy that changes when the monitoring contract changes hands. A wrong number in a signed controlled document means the crew cannot book the isolate and either delays the job or, worse, isolates without booking and turns out the brigade.
blocking.fix: Confirm the current QFD-contracted alarm monitoring provider, the contact number and the isolation duration threshold against Queensland Fire Department's own published alarm monitoring / alarm isolation material before this SWMS is issued. Then restructure so the volatile facts live in one place: keep the obligation in permits[2] and steps[2] controls[2] in words ('Book the ASE isolate with the QFD-contracted alarm monitoring provider before you isolate, and write the isolation reference on the permit'), and move the contractor name, phone number and duration threshold into a single dated line in references marked with the date it was checked, so it is obvious when it has gone stale. Keep the substantive controls that surround it — confirming the occupier's alternative protection arrangement is in place before isolating, and arranging any long-isolation approval beforehand rather than at 4pm — they are the right controls regardless of who answers the phone.

blocking.field: steps[4] 'Set up the work position — access, height, and the exclusion zone below' — hazards and controls; and emergency
blocking.problem: The step covers falls, dropped slag and the drop zone, but never names the mechanism that kills EWP operators most often: the operator crushed or trapped between the basket and structure overhead. The document comes within a word of it — hazards[2] says the EWP risks 'striking sprinkler pipe and services overhead' — but treats that only as damage to the pipe, not as the operator pinned against it. A plant room ceiling is exactly the environment for it: sprinkler mains, ducts, cable tray, beams, all at basket height. There is also no rescue provision. controls[4] requires a spotter only 'wherever forklifts or vehicles move', so a plant room EWP job with no traffic legitimately has nobody at ground level, and nobody who can reach the emergency lowering controls. The emergency section covers harness suspension trauma (correctly, and against a verified ANZCOR guideline) but has nothing for an operator trapped in a basket, where sustained pressure on the chest kills in minutes and the harness advice does not apply.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[4] hazards: 'Operator crushed or trapped between the EWP basket and overhead structure — sprinkler mains, ducts, cable tray, beams — with the controls unreachable.' Add an administrative control to steps[4]: 'A second person stays at ground level for the whole time the basket is elevated, is briefed on the emergency lowering controls and the machine key is accessible to them. This is separate from the fire watch and it is not optional because there is no forklift traffic.' Add an engineering or administrative control on approach: survey the overhead before elevating, mark the services in the travel path, and no travelling with the basket elevated in the plant room. Add to emergency: 'OPERATOR TRAPPED IN AN EWP BASKET: do not wait. Use the ground emergency lowering controls to relieve the pressure, ring 000 immediately, and keep talking to them. Sustained pressure on the chest kills in minutes.' Add to siteSpecificPrompts: 'Who is on the ground while the basket is up, and have they been shown the emergency lowering controls?'

blocking.field: steps[8] 'Fire watch during the work, and for 60 minutes after the last spark' — residualRisk
blocking.problem: initialRisk is extreme, every one of the five controls is administrative, and residualRisk is stated as medium. This does not breach the app rule as written (that rule bites only on admin/PPE-only with a residual of low), which is why I am raising it as minor rather than serious. But it is the step where the building has no detection and no suppression, the hazard is a smoulder that by definition has not shown itself yet, and the entire residual rests on one person continuing to pay attention. There is no engineering or isolation control in the step at all — the interim protection that would justify a medium sits back in steps[3] and is not carried forward. Compare steps[9], which is also administrative-only from extreme, but where the controls are verification steps with a second-person countersign that genuinely close the loop; step 8 has no equivalent backstop.
blocking.fix: Either raise steps[8] residualRisk to high, which is the honest reading while the fire system is off and would also tell a technician reading the row that this is not a step to get casual about — or keep medium and add the missing non-administrative control that justifies it, carried forward explicitly rather than by implication: the extinguishers and charged hose reel at the work position and the sealed penetrations from steps[3] remain in place for the full watch and are not packed up until the watch is stood down, plus a temporary standalone battery smoke alarm sited in the work area where the room will stay isolated after the crew leaves. Adding that as an 'engineering' or 'isolate' level control and keeping medium is the better fix, because it changes what happens on site rather than just changing a word on the form.
